samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with William Brown was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: -- Museum in Plymouth, Michigan, as part of our Veterans History Project. We're here to interview a local veteran, Mr. William Brown. Mr. Brown, could you please tell us what you did before you went into the service?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Well, I was trained as a machinist and an automotive mechanic.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: And you worked at that or were you in school?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: I worked as a machinist, as the war started. And I was deferred from the draft for 18 months due to my machinist experience.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Experience. Okay. And were you working locally here in Plymouth?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: In the Detroit area.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Detroit area. Where was that? Do you recall?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: The name of the company?

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Yes. Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Was -- the name of the company was the Anderson Machining Company. As correct -- as close as I can come to it.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, okay. Where was that located?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: It was in -- I believe Highland Park.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Mm-hmm. Okay. So you were talking about Detroit. You're really talking about almost downtown Detroit.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Mm-hmm, mm-hmm. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: And you worked at a machine shop where you were automobile-related?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: No. It was all the -- it was all war material.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: War material?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah. It was all war material. There was one- and two-piece items for special events, I guess.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Because we weren't told what it was for. And I was the (inaudible) to do my job at it.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: What kind of -- give us an idea what you made that would be --

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Well, it was a lot of castings.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Castings?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: A lot of castings that had to be machined and -- and finished as a product. Heat-treated and things along that line.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Something special then?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Everything was a specialty --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: That was during --

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: -- that I can recall.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: It was part of the war effort, though?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: All war effort. And that's what gave me my 18 months of deferment from being drafted.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Okay. So what happened after 18 months? You got --

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Well, then the draft board says, "Bill, it's time for you to volunteer for whatever service you'd like to volunteer for."

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Okay. They gave you a choice?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: They gave me a choice. Really. As I remember, it was in Pontiac, Michigan that I had to report to -- report to. So I opted to -- well, they give you a list of what things you could opt to volunteer for. So I -- Army Engineers.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Army of Engineers. Army Corps of Engineers.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Army Corps of Engineers.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: All right. Now, what were you going to do there?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: That is a good question. They specialized -- as I understand it, they were picking people throughout the service to fill particular jobs that they had in mind for that times because the regiment was formed in the early part of 1943, and it was a -- listed as a regiment service, and then it was redesigned as a regiment special service.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: The 361st Engineer Special Service.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Engineer Special Service.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Okay. This is the outfit you went into?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: That's the one I went into.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: And you went to training, didn't you?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah. From there, we went to -- well, we started out in Michigan and -- over in Battle Creek, and then we transferred to Camp Claiborne, Louisiana.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Okay. You went from Fort Custer --

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: From Custer to Camp Claiborne, Louisiana.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Okay. What did you do at Camp Claiborne?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Then at Camp Claiborne, Louisiana, I started my basic training there. I believe I completed most of it, and then I was sent to advanced training in machinery -- and machinist in Granite City, Illinois.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, okay. Closer to home?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: For a three-month training of special. And you had to pass an entrance exam, and I passed that within the time that was allotted, which was -- worked with a file, a hammer and a saw and a few other things. Very limited amount of tools. They wanted to see your ability to produce something if you were limited with the amount of equipment you had.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Right, right.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: So that was it. And from there, back to Camp Claiborne.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Okay. Back to Camp Claiborne. Now, you went back there as -- what? As part of the --

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: After the training, I went back right into the Company C, and that was it.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Okay. With the 361st.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah. 361st.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Okay. So after your training period after Fort Claiborne or Camp Claiborne at the time, where did you go from there?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: We stayed right there. And we continued some training, and one day, I walked into the first sergeant's headquarters. I was always looking for something to do because I was trained as a machinist, and we had a big machinery truck that they had, special trailer and everything. Put through in the training, basic training and the advanced training and explosives and bridge building, airport landing fields, which we had a lot of pictures of. I decided, well, I had ridden a motorcycle when I was a young kid. So I said to the first sergeant, "You know, it would be a good time -- you need a motorcycle rider?" He says, "Yes." So I said, "Well, I'll sign up." He said, "Where did you ever ride?" I told him, and I made a sta -- few statements.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And so then they sent me to motorcycle school.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Is that right? They had a school for that?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah. Not a -- not a big school, but a little -- a little training on a motorcycle. I don't even remember what it was, but it was training.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: It was a local training?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah. Then they trained us in convoy duty, you know, where we'd have convoys, and motorcycle riders would stop the traffic and stuff.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: That's where I had my one motorcycle accident.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Where was that at?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: In Louisiana. I believe -- I can't tell you the location, but I think it was in Louisiana. It may have been in Alabama. Who knows?

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: But it was down South. Hot.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Hot. Yeah. Okay.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah. So that was that. And then of course I had some motor pool training, so I did a little motor pool work. And then I thought -- one of the highlights of it, they -- I walked into the first sergeant's office one day, and they said, "The officers would like to have an officer's orderly, and they pay."

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Hmm.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And I said, "Well, how much do they pay?" And I don't remember what it was, but anyway, I got the job.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Is that right?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: So I was officer's orderly that way. So from then on, I was always known as "Ass Brown," (inaudible) "Brown Nose."

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Brown nose?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: (laughter) Because you remember them service things. "Brown nose."

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Okay. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: But --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: What did you -- what was the duties of an officer orderly? What was that?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Well, you had to get up, make sure that their meals were there in the morning and that their -- anything that we had to tell them, that was allowed to be told. And also had to straighten up their quarters. So when they left, whatever they were doing, you had everything back in shape for them, so when they came back.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: So it was a rather -- nothing big -- not a big job.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Not a big job.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: But they paid a few pennies, and I was married, and so I sent the money home.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: So --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Yeah. How much were you making in the service at the time? Do you remember?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: I took -- well, as I recall, I took 10 dollars a month for myself all the time I was in the Army. As far as I can recall. The rest, I sent home to my wife.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: So were you an orderly through to the end of the war?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, what happened?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: It was just a short job.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, you had -- you did a lot of jobs, didn't you?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah. That was a short job. I was always noted for always trying to get another job because I hate sitting around. So anyway, that's the story of that. And then we had a lot of dress parades and stuff. And I always -- a little fun story there. Dress parade. On the co -- regiment as far as I can remember, and the colonel and all his officers in charge were all up there, observing the dressing and stuff. And it just so happened that I wanted to go home on a leave with the Red Cross because my wife had had their first child -- our first child.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, okay. All right.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And I was declined.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: So I don't know what the -- what the -- what it was, but we were in a close-order drill that day, and as we were marching forward to the -- towards the colonel, somebody said to the rear "march," and I didn't get it. And I almost run into the colonel. And he said, "Well, soldier, get back in step." So that's the only story I really remember about that. But I was rather disillusioned that I couldn't go home to see --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Yeah. You had your mind elsewhere, for sure.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Don't blame you.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: So that's about -- so a lot of other little exciting things down there that I can't recall. Other than that we did a lot of things on the Mississippi deltas as we were waiting for further orders. Cutting down weeds that the natives in the area thought we were absolutely out of our mind along the dikes because they were just going to grow right back up.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: What kind of weeds were they?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Big tall weeds that we could --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Still there?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Still there. They never will get rid of them.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: There's a name for it, and I can't remember. A friend of mine from -- but it's -- gosh. It grows everywhere. It's like a vine. And it grows everywhere. And I'm trying to remember the name of it. I was just down there last year.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Don't get cut because I got cut by it. And I got one of -- the sap in one of my little cuts on my legs, and it took months for it to heal.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah. Some sort of a reaction to it.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: There's something to it. I forget what --

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Then we also would get a chance to go into -- I think twice we got a chance to go into New -- New --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: New Orleans?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: -- into New Orleans.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: New Orleans. Yes.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And you know, the other thing that was nice was Port Sulphur, Alabama, was they had oysters there on the half shell for -- six oysters on two slices of bread for a quarter. That was one of the highlights.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, is that right?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: What a deal.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: That was Port Sulphur, Miss -- I think it was Alabama or Mississippi. One or the other.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: But that was interesting. And I had never been in a place in my life where there was so many mosquitoes.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Carry you away.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: You just couldn't put your arm against the bed at night at all because if you did, your arm was like this in the morning.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: I know.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: So --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: So you had the netting, right? You had to sleep with the netting around you?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah. I put my shoes against the side.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Yeah. To keep it down.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And the fiddler crabs would push all the --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: (laughter) The fiddler crabs?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Fiddler crabs. One crab -- one claw.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And if they -- millions of them, popping when you walk at night. You had to run at night because there were so many mosquitoes, but anything that -- anybody that smoked would push their cigarettes or anything down the little hole. He'd push it back out and then -- always in trouble.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Little things like that. Now it seems like humor. Then, it was like a little humor.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Yeah. I understand. Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: But that's the extent of all that. And we traveled around quite a bit.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Okay. Where did you travel around? You brought your canteen cup here.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Well, that's -- that's a different story. That --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Okay. Let's --

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: -- canteen cup is more or less something that when we went -- finally left the United States.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Okay. Your -- as a unit?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah. As a unit.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Where did you go?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Well, we were -- this is interesting. They put us on a train in Louisiana, and I think we went all -- it seems like we went to the coast, to the West Coast of the United States, before we went to New York, where our debark --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: That doesn't make sense.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Where we departed was from --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: You were in New Orleans, right, or --

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah, in that area.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: In that area?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Camp Claiborne. And we left there, and it seems like we went farther west to go east, if you know military.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: So we went -- we wound up in New York City, and then we shipped out of there. And we had a day or two in New York City.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: When was this? Do you remember? Timing --

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Probably would have been about 1944.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah. '44. I'm pretty sure. And we got on board the Dutch ship USS -- no. The Dutch ship was NEW AMSTERDAM.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I know several fellows that have been on that ship.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah. NEW AMSTERDAM.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: It was a liner. It was a --

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: It was a big liner. It was -- it was in the class of the French and the Amer -- and the English, QUEEN MARY and the (inaudible). I -- my opinion of that ship -- and maybe it's -- I'm wrong at this, but I would swear that was the dirtiest ship I was ever on in my life.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, gosh.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And I say that because nothing worked.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Nothing worked.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Even the latrines. So anyway, we crossed the Atlantic Ocean, uneventful and with all of the regiment. Then we wound up getting off in Gourock, Scotland.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Where is that? Scotland.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Scotland. We had to get off on tenders and go ashore. And I walked up the hill with my duffel bag and whatever else I was carrying. And at the top of the hill was the Salvation Army. I always remember that. And there was a young lady there handing out coffee and donuts. And I says, "Oh, we're in England." She says, "England be damned. This is Scotland."

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: (laughter) Gotta be careful.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: "This is Scotland."

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And so I didn't say anything anymore. I thought, well, I'd be better more of a diplomat than this, so anyway, they put us on the train and we went -- trained all the way to Southampton, England.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, okay. Now, Southampton's a port?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah. Southampton was the departure port. From there, Southampton. I can tell you --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Okay. Read the cup.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: From England, we got on a ship called the KING ROYAL.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: The KING ROYAL.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And sailed to -- in the area of Omaha Beach, Cherbourg, in that area.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Depart there.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: What -- what time of year was this?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: That would have been in October of 19 --

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: '44. Yeah. It was after D-Day.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, yeah. That was --

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: So we still had trouble getting up that beach. The mud was so thick at that time, that we had -- our trucks and everything were a pain in the neck. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Okay. So now you're in France.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah. And in France, we did a various -- various number of things, pumping -- I don't know what the other companies did in our regiment, but I have a history of it in my book here, but --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: But it's too hard to read. It's faded out. Company C was involved with a number of projects from anywhere's from roads to gravel pits to -- that was part of my job. I remember rebuilding a stone crusher for the road-building, you know, because the Germans had destroyed the -- the equipment.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And I remember arguing with the French people there so badly that -- we didn't know what we were doing. And I always remember the French would say, "Don't tell the Yanks they can't do it because they'll do it anyway."

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: (laughter) They knew you, didn't they?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah. So anyway, that's what we did.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Then we -- we -- one of the -- one of the major projects was building a huge hospital --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Hmm.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: -- and setting up the -- all the equipment for a hospital. And that's what we meant by "special service." In our -- in our -- in our group, in that Company C, so that we may not go to the front and fight with the infantry, but we would be the -- supported in the back --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: -- whatever they had, or we had to build the hospitals and build everything to make these things work, so the whole -- the big picture. You know. So the Air Force was there. And I remember the gliders and everything being towed away and towed over -- a number, a number of things went on there. But some of the hospitals and things, I thought was one of our major projects in our company.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Where were they being built at? Do you recall?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: They were built in an old French area where they -- actually, I think it was a -- what do you call the horse regiment? Where they had all the horses and everything?

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: The cavalry?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: The cavalry. I think it was an old cavalry. It seemed like it was an old cavalry because --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Old cavalry?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: -- because it was in Mourmelon-le-Grand.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: I remember that we had to clean out everything, all the buildings, and restore it all. We installed huge washing machines, huge dryers. Everything. Huge generators.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: For the linens and all that, you'd have to --

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Oh, everything for that. And then we also -- the other -- a lot of people worked in the actual building, setting up the hospital rooms, which I didn't do.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: I was more or less in the other -- in all the engineering. The heated area and the motor pool and stuff like that.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Yeah. Sure.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And in the meantime, I rode a motorcycle for dispatch driver --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: -- when I wasn't doing that.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Can you tell us what a dispatch rider does or what's their job?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Dispatch rider is every day, you receive a -- what the devil do they call that form? It's a form that you get that allows you for 24 hours --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Pass?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: A pass?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Not a pass. A pass allows you to go. This is a -- like a -- you have an order to -- say that you are delivering packages, or you're delivering mail, or you're delivering orders. Or whatever it is.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: A dispatch, like.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And I did this for a number of days, when I wasn't doing other things.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: So we did that in the winter. And then -- when we could ride in the winter. When we couldn't ride in the winter, why, fine. But we did that a lot. Rode Jeeps. I had motor pool duties, small engine duties. Some -- whatever duties that -- required in the area, that motor pool area.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Right, right.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And so that kept me busy.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And we had a lot of -- a lot of things go on.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And we had -- some of the roads, they had what they call a red ball service where the trucks were carrying war material to the front. We had to make sure our part of the roads were going so that those truck drivers could keep moving. The red ball service, as I remember.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: I worked for red ball services in Vietnam.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Did you?

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: We took things up to the field. We would get -- three-quarter ton or Jeep, whatever was needed.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: 6x6 GMC.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Yeah. Two tons. We'd take them up to the units, whatever they needed. It was a red ball, 24 hours. Whenever they needed, they'd get it in 24 hours.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Well, the motorcycle allowed me to travel a lot of places that I can't even remember. But I had delivered -- I would deliver whatever it was. It would be messages, it would be orders, or it would be material or parts or whatever. And you had to find your way around.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: This is in France, right?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah. In France.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: So you had to know a little bit of French?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Well, I learned a few words, but the one thing was you could stop at any Army camp or anyplace you wanted to start -- stop, and they -- as long as you had your dispatch for that day, it was good for 24 hours. You could eat there, get messages, service of any kind you needed. And so this is how I got around.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Okay. And I know. And one of the things I remember, too, very distinctly was watching -- I think the Germans surrendered, and they arrived in Reims, France.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: I happened to be riding down the road when the -- on the motorcycle going into Reims through a checkpoint --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: -- when I saw all the stuff happening.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Describe to us what you saw.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: I thought it was -- more -- if I remember right, it was an aircraft and stuff like. I thought, "What the -- what's that type of aircraft doing over here?" You know.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: It was German, right?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: German aircraft?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: As far as I remember.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: I saw pictures of that.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: It's vaguely -- it's a vague part of my memory. But I do remember saying, "Oh, boy." All this stuff going on.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: One of our GIs that was in here showed me some pictures of that aircraft and also of the aircraft that was in Japan during their -- so they had these Japanese planes coming in --

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: I missed that.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: -- for the surrender. So this is in Reims, France. You saw the Germans coming in for the formal surrender. Okay.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. We were in -- I made many trips into Reims. Just a side story on that. The checkpoint was -- when I'd get some orders to go to Reims, why, a particular day, I'd take some. Maybe I took the mail or something. But anyway, the MPs on the checkpoint got to know me pretty regularly. And I'd check in. And on the way out, I'd slow down by the checkpoint. And then I'd gun it and go through.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And really what it was -- and they told me later on. They would chase me with their motor -- with their Jeep. Never catch me. We had the motorcycle upgraded a little bit from -- from friends in the motor pool. But when I'd go through again, they would -- nothing would be said. It was a diversion.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: It was a game. It was a game.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: It was a game. And we would just spin off for a while or two, and then they'd go back to the -- but --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: (laughter) They knew you were coming, too, didn't they?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah. So they got to know me and it was --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: That's interesting.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Side stories again on that, we -- of course, riding the motorcycle, you're on your own. You're out on the various parts of wherever you're going. And I don't know. I can't even name all the places we had to go to. But once in a while, I'd see a broken-down motorcycle or something on the road and a Frenchman standing there, and I'd stop. I'd watch him pretty close, but I'd stop. See his motorcycle broken. Maybe I could help him so I'd help a couple of them, you know, get started or get going. And I remember one of them always paid me off in cognac.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: So I had a couple of bottles of cognacs when I'd go back to the base after I'd come by this area sometimes where he was. And so --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Made you a pretty popular guy with that cognac in hand, right?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Well, gave that to a couple of guys that were -- and by the way, just to back up, when -- I was 22, 23, and you were considered to be an old man by all.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: At 22? Yeah?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: 22. We were what we call -- they called us "old men." And the guys were in their late 20s or early 20s. We were not 18. So that was interesting. But the cognac, I gave it to different fellows. And once in a while, we'd take them someplace.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Once in a while, the motorcycle -- an Army motorcycle, Harley-Davidson, has one seat. And the MPs stop you and you've got two guys on it, you're in trouble. But one guy always wanted to go halfway to Epernay when I was in -- the champagne center of the world at the time. And so he rode there one day with me, on the back, and I let him off. And the MP or somebody said, "You know you're sup" -- I said, "Yeah. I know that. But he just -- he was walking. He was tired. So I gave him a short ride." But anyway, we had about five or six motorcycles in our group, too, in the motor pool. They were English motorcycles, Nortons, Triumphs. And the lieutenants would ride the pipeline with those bike -- motorcycles.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: The pipeline?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: The pipeline of oil and gas.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, really? Check them out?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah. They would ride the pipelines. And the only one that rode the Harley-Davidson was the captain of the regiment and myself because he allowed nobody else to ride the Harley. And the Harley was not an easy bike compared to the French.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: The French -- or not the French bike, but --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: The English.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: -- English bikes are easy. Single cylinder, real light. You could walk alongside and run, ride with them. The Harley, we had to put a hand clutch on it so we could do that because you can't ride in the mud or you can't stand it up. If you have to get off and walk on the side of it, with the foot clutch, you can't do it.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Can't do it. Right, right, right.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: So --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Never thought of that. Yeah. Okay.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: It worked out. So those are the basic things, and there's a lot of other stuff that I can't recall. When the Battle of the Bulge work came about, they came to our regiment, and they practically decimated the regiment to get more people for the infantry or for the thing. But somehow, I was overlooked to become a frontline person. Maybe it was due to my ability to do all the motor pool and keep all the other stuff and anything. And then of course I had had that foot injured on the motorcycle, which isn't good for marching, although I don't think it bothered me that much. But who knows what kept me from going there. But we were background of it, the Battle of the Bulge, which we were in the area, but I did not have to go up there and fight in the front lines on it, but we were very instrumental in the back side of it.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Okay. What did you guys do as --

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Just keep things going.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Keep things going?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Keep things going. Whatever you need to do. Keep going. I can't remember all that stuff. It's vague. You know.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Kept you busy.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Busy.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. So what else happened after that?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Well, finally the war ended. Why, they decided that we did not have enough time to -- and points to -- at least I didn't, and the regiment didn't, as far as I know, the majority of the people in the regiment. So they boxed us -- well, we had convoys to southern France, Marseilles, France. And some people went on the train, and some people went by convoy. And that was the most treacherous ride we ever had. We had lost some people on the ride because it -- over the accidents, trucks, and it was icy winter. Anyway, staged out in Marseilles, spent a few days in Marseilles, swam in the Mediterranean with the jellyfish. Left Marseilles on the USS LORALINE.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: LORALINE.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: 5,000 people got on the USS LORALINE. And I always remember this. When we got -- I don't remember whether we got on board or whether we was processed before we got on board. Everybody had to turn in all moneys that they had, and they gave each one of us a 10 dollars American dollar bill. Imagine five guys -- guys with 10 dollar bill. Crap game time.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: (inaudible)

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And the -- the minister -- what the devil? The chaplain would come down every now and again on one of the crap games. I never did like the crap -- he'd come by, and he'd say, "Well, this is for the chaplain for the day."

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Take the pot. But anyway, we sailed from the -- on the USS LORALINE, which is the first time we got into good (inaudible) wet and all that stuff.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Been a long time.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Sailed into the Panama Canal. Went through the canal. Got off there for 24 hours to a USO service place where they had all kinds of entertainment, bands and people to dance with, American ladies and nurses and everybody. And we got back on the ship and sailed out into the -- I remember we went out on the Pacific, and we were in some of the islands. And then we finally wound up in the Bay of Manila, at Manila, the Philippines. We sat out there, and then we finally got off board in Manila. And we -- I wound up in the little town with our company called San Jacinto. And that was not too far from one of the airfields there. And we did a lot of things around there, but that was -- To me, I was always sick. Always had dysentery. Always carried a bottle of (inaudible) all the time. Went to town a few times with whatever it was. I forget where it was, Manila or whatever, but we did a lot of air -- a lot of work around airfields there and a lot of staging. A lot of walking in the jungles, and it's a little -- the war was on, but we did what I call just reconnoitering out on the -- you know, go out and look the countryside over on patrol.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: We found a lot of places in the mountains where people had had haciendas and things, but they would all been destroyed. It was still the foundations and things there, cement, and a lot of -- a lot of destruction. Tremendous destruction. Same in Europe when we were there. But one day on the patrol, which we were just walking up and down through the side of these mountains and looking around -- looking at these haciendas and everything, and I hear this sound going off (demonstrating) like a little motor running. And we carried on, started looking for it. And we finally got in a little clearing in the jungle area there. And here's a grass hut, and there's an electric generator running. And on the -- and there's a table in the middle with some rickety chairs and on -- and then it says cold beer for a dollar and a half.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: (laughter) You're kidding.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Honest to God.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: In the middle of the jungle?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Turns out it's our GI beer in the -- the 32 beer?

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: You know what the hardest thing was? Trying to find a dollar and a half.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, gosh.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: But we did. Amongst us -- and we -- to this day, I can see that cold bottle of beer sweating.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: In the middle of that jungle. And that was -- I remember that distinctly. And then from there, we went on. But we used to -- in the Philippines there, they issued you the GI beer, G32 beer.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: 32 beer.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Which you couldn't get it cold, so -- you had so much a month. I forget what it was, but they used to put it in the rivers. And the rivers were only about that deep, and the water was warm, and there were water buffaloes and --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: -- everything else in the river. And various things, but -- And the interesting -- one other -- I try to keep it more interesting because there's a lot of destruction, a lot of other stuff. People know about war and stuff. But one of the things I always remark was a funeral procession in the Philippines at San Jacinto. They're all in a line. They're carrying this person in a small box, and they're playing the song "Tie My Tail" -- that "Monkey Tie His Tail Around the Flagpole." A real upbeat type for a funeral. Some of the people -- some of the soldiers would try to drink -- and this is true all over -- drink different things that would make them sicker than a dog. They had all kinds of problems. From there, we got staged, and we got on an LST, No. 23, and sailed to the -- we left there, and the war was over. By the way, when we were on the USS LORALINE going across the Pacific, the war ended.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, is that right? (End of video clip)

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: The war ended, and we carried the ship -- you can see the trail in the ocean of the powers and things. And about a half hour after that, it seemed they turned around, and everybody thought, "Whoa. We're going home." So they did that for -- I would -- I don't know the time, but say an hour, and turned around again.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, gosh.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And so we wound up in the Philippine Islands. Well, back up a little bit. In the Philippine Islands, of course, we were in an area where there was a lot of Japanese airplanes. I remember some of the Jap airplanes laying around. They were directional. And the -- the night king -- the night, the Black Widows. I remember those stacked up.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: P-61s and other aircraft. And I brought home a ring called out of a -- carved out of a Japanese tank -- or a Japanese propeller. And then I brought home a letter opener made by the Filipinos with all the -- Philippine Islands 1945, made out of a Japanese tank spring. The blade, the crossbar, the brass was out of that. And the only thing on it, the caribou was from a caribou, the handle. So that's still mine.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: That's kind of neat.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah. And it's still there. But when the ship turned around and we headed back -- of course started back up a little bit, we went on to Japan or I mean to the Philippine Islands. And then from there, we started -- as I just said, we got back through the Philippines and were headed out into the China Sea. I think it was probably in process of a few days or what, but anyway, we were on the outskirts of the hurricane that wiped out Okinawa almost.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, wow.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And we were in the seas that I've never been in. And at that time, I thought, "None of us will ever survive." Because the ship would hit these tremendous waves, and it actually would -- the bow would go up. And then when the bow would come down, the whole ship would shudder. And all our trucks and everything were tied to the deck and our heavy equipment like the big Caterpillars and everything was down below.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And you could see the chains tighten up and then loosen up. We did lose all our gasoline. Our barrels of gasoline went over. But -- and we had the Cats -- I say "Cats"; the Caterpillars. And the bow up in the ship break loose. They'd slip back and forth, and we had to go down there and block them off and keep from tearing out the ship.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: That's a dangerous thing to do in a storm.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And we had people on there that had joined us in the Philippines that were just newcomers from the States and very little time at sea. And they were just down below. And you could hardly eat anyway. But anyway, we're down there. We'd play poker for no limit because we never thought we'd --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Get out of there? (laughter)

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: -- get out of that sea, out of that ocean. Oh, God. I have pictures of that. And the ship. One little episode on board that ship was sort of -- it stands out in my mind because for lack of something to do, my -- my particular piece of equipment was a truck on deck tied next to the rail. And at times, we'd sleep up there, when we could. If we could, we'd find a place where we could sleep. And everything that we owned for our own stuff was there. So one day, I'm just sitting there, and I decided, you know, I'm going to clean my rifle for something to do. So I cleaned out my rifle. Cleaned it all up. Put it back in the -- and wouldn't you know that they had inspection.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: No kidding.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: I don't know how many other fellows, but I think I was one of the only ones that had a clean rifle. Well, from then on, it was always, "Don't ask Brown. Brown knows when they're going to have" --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Do you know what that does to you in a bunch of guys?

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, God. Yeah. They were unrelenting.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah. So there's a lot of stories, though. But then we --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: You've got some pictures of the storm? We'll take a look at them.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: You brought your pictures with you?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah. I got some of the pictures. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Let's take a look at them. I'll stop the film for a second. (Break) We're looking now at a picture of the ship. This is No. 23, LST No. 23. And that's around something, China. But this is a ship?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: That's in the China Sea.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: China Sea. And this is the ship you were on that was during this big storm you were talking about?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah, the typhoon that --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: -- wiped out -- almost wiped out --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Doesn't look very -- I've got a guy, Staff Sergeant St. Vincent, France. Oh, okay. You've got a mishmash of pictures here. Some are from France --

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Oh, they're all (inaudible). They're not in order.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Don't take them in order. That's --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: These are just pictures you had --

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: My kids did this.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, your kids did this?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Years ago.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: They just took pictures, put them where they fit.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, okay. In the album then.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: (inaudible) album. Then the rest of them come along and stole them.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Because you've got a Philippines funeral. There's a picture of the Philippine funeral.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: That's that where they were playing the --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: This is when they were playing that song?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: For the monkeys to wrap their tail?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: (inaudible)

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Isn't that something? Sort of upbeat song for a funeral. It's kind of a little different, isn't it? LST No. 23. Now, "LST" stood for what?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: This is -- "leaving" is the caption on the bottom. It's leaving some bay.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And there --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Let's see. White Beach, Lausanne, going to Japan. And it's going to Japan on October 23, 1945. "LST" stood for "landing ship tank"; is that right?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Okay. It looks like a picture of you about to bayonet -- bayonet somebody there in front of a tent. Fooling around?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: He wanted to eat my pie. (laughter) No kidding. I don't know. We were just joking around.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Just joking around.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Somewheres in the south, new Texas or Louisiana or someplace like that. I'm not sure where.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: The fourth landing, huh?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah. It tells it in the history, but -- And we had to build this field to get out of there.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: You had to build a field to get the plane out?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Build a field and lay that steel.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Okay. I see that. Yeah. The grids on the ground there?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah. See how it's bent?

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Yeah. To get that crew out? My goodness. Now, where was this at?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: It was down in -- it was somewheres in the southern states. It would have either been Louisiana, Texas or -- (inaudible) dinner.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Okay. This is you as an officer -- officer orderly, right?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yep. Camp Claiborne.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Okay. In Cape Claiborne, Louisiana.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Looking at right now is aboard that LST 23, right?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: On the way to Japan.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: On the way to Japan.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: When the weather was nice.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Much nicer. You had a nice sunny day when you took that picture.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: I forgot his name. I'll tell you that in a minute, though.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: That was today, though?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Today. It's going to be a news -- going to be an article in the paper.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: So you --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Tell me the story again. I'm going to put it on tape now. So this car, it was brought into your shop?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: It was -- yeah. They -- they -- the brother of the owner of the automobile asked me to look at the engine, which was a 1941 Straight Eight Buick, beautiful shape, for oil leaks. And the story goes that this car was in the attack of Pearl Harbor, and he has in the trunk the original piece of windshield with the hole in it.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: No kidding.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And the fellow that owned the car --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: The bullet hole, you're talking about?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Bullet hole.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Bullet hole. Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Bullet hole in the windshield.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And the person that owned the car was a pilot. And he ended here, along with four other pilots. This is the story that I have from the gentleman that told me today, so that -- we have to go by that.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And supposedly the -- he was shot down and one -- and still to this day, they have never found his body or the airplane.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Aw.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And he was one of the first pilots in the -- killed in -- killed in Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And they still -- and at 60th anniversary in Hawaii, they had the Japanese pilots come.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, no kidding.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And this is his story to me today. And I imagine it will be in the newspaper because it's supposed to be. The story goes that the leading commander of the first air group -- I don't know which one or he didn't know each other -- was supposedly shot down by one of our airplanes. But this particular pilot that's now alive 60 years said that he -- (Interruption)

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: I'm sorry. Go ahead.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: He said that the Japanese pilot said no, that he was not shot down, that he had been shot at, but then he turned around and he shot down that airplane, and it was this fellow's brother.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: That's the story that was told by this particular man, and I can't recall his name.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, that's something.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And it's Shiffley or something. But it's -- it's a --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Interesting story.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And they're still looking for him. Because they -- there's none in the Hawaiian harbor. There's no airplanes left wherever he said that they've been looking for airplanes, Japanese or Americans.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Is that right?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: So the story will be in --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Have you been to Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: I was -- we sailed through new -- Pearl Harbor when we were on the USS LORALINE.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: We stopped there, but I never got off. I could have got off, not knowing that if you had a relative there, you could have got off. And my brother-in-law was on the police department there, but I --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, yeah?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: But I forgot about it and didn't know where he was. So anyway. But that's -- that's the story of that.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Interesting. Interesting story.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: But that's -- but anyway, the car's there, and it's amazing, beautiful car. It's got the Hawaiian license plate on the front.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: So why is it doing here in Michigan? What's the purpose of the car being here?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Well, he's had it --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Part of a collection?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: He's had it at many shows. Well, this -- of course, he's the brother of the owner, so --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: -- he just keeps the car and drives it. And it's -- they've had it in the family over 60 years.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Yeah. That's something.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Nice car. Nice shape. Hawaiian car.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Kind of a memorial to his brother then, isn't it?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah. And he has all the papers of when his brother bought it. It came from Alabama, state of Alabama. Registration.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah. Fantastic.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Isn't that something?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah. But it's all history. That's my dad when he was in World War I.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Is he in the picture? I want to see what he looks like. Can you lift it up there --

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Just take a gander at your dad --

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: -- Navy on a battleship.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: What battleship was he on?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: I'll be darned if I know. (laughter)

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: But he was in the Navy. You've got a fellow standing next to him. Who was that?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: One of his friends, I believe.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: That was a -- it looks like a Army uniform, though.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Well, it could have been a friend.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Yeah. Isn't that something? Do you remember the ship's name or --

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: I do, but I don't remember at the moment.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Offhand?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Uh-uh. It was a battleship. And he was a bugler.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: On board ship. And there was none in our family that could even carry a tune, let alone blow one. We landed in Japan on the US -- on the -- a LST 23.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And then we motored. And I don't remember the beach we landed on, but then we motored to a place called Osaka.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And we lived in a emperor's palace in the moat in Osaka.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Is that right?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah. And we all got fleas.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Fleas? No kidding.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Had to be deloused. That was interesting, as I recall. And we did a lot of things around Osaka. And finally we left Osaka, and we went to a town called Kyoto, the City of the Seven Shrines. And we -- if I was to go through the history, we probably did more in Japan in the city of Kyoto than anything else and restoring and building stuff. It's -- doing all kinds of restoration and buildings and hospitals and stuff like that, so -- Did I move over?

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: No. I did. I'm sorry. I have you on -- there we go. So --

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And Japan was a very interesting country because when we first landed there, why, the story was by the Japanese government that the Americans wanted to rape all the women and murder everybody. But at two weeks, I think we were eating out of their hands, the way we are as Americans, you know.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: But we traveled around. I did a lot of traveling around there, going to the various little towns, checking on supplies and various things that we should control. Groceries, sugar, flour and all that stuff.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Rations. There was a rationing system going on?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Now, this is when MacArthur was in charge of Japan, wasn't it?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah. That's right. But we were in there first part. We were in there in October. So in October and November, December. And of course all that time. And then -- I remember going to these various towns and meeting up with the local mayors of the town. And they would put on a dinner or a meal for us, but we never ate their food. We always carried our own bread and stuff. But the women were never allowed into the meetings. They always served the meals on -- at an entrance to a doorway.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And then the men would take care of everything. We did a lot of that type things and a lot of restoration. Oh, I can't go about everything and (inaudible) --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: -- and stuff. But it had to do with even building -- restoring hospital rooms. Restoring hotel rooms, hotel lobbies, you know, things that were -- Because Kyoto supposedly had never been bombed because it was the City of Seven Shrines. That was interesting there because we did a lot of things that -- visited a lot of their temples and --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: -- and various things.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Probably one of the most historical places in Japan.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And -- stop it for a second.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Sure. (Break)

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: So this is you?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Ringing the huge bell in one of those Buddha temples.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: In Kyoto, Japan?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Mm-hmm. I have pictures of us having a meal with the Japanese. I can't find it.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Now, these were the Japanese soldiers that were -- or the American soldiers?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: No. Those are Japanese.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Japanese.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah. We didn't know their language, but we get very good with sign language.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: They -- we'd -- we'd had bread with them. We'd bring our own bread.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And we would have bread, and we'd sit on the side of these hills, and I have pictures of them, and I can't seem to put my hand on them --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: That's fine.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: -- of these people sitting, having bread with us. Not -- not military men, just Japanese civilian --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Civilians. Yeah. Did you see after a couple weeks they got over their fear of the GIs?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah. More or less, they were doing our laundry, it seemed like, and everything else for us. We did a few culture changes over there, I thought. Because it was amazing. The women did most of the work. And they would carry everything on their back. And we'd get on the local public transportation, and the men would get on, sit down, and the women would stand up with all this stuff on their back, whether it would be children or whether it would -- we would just merely pick the men up very nicely, set the women down in the chair and make the man stand up.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Is that right?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: That's all we did. We tried -- didn't make any fights, just did it nicely. And that, I think, changed a lot of their thinking.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: It sure changed a lot since then.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: We have respect more of the women than normal people do, you know.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Anyway, that was basically what we did in Japan. And we -- there's two -- in Japan, there's two things to drink over there. There's some No. 1 sake and No. 2 sake, which is a rice or a barley sake, which is -- you ever have sake? It's in a little glass. Well, there was a lot of that over there. And people bought it, and some of the guys black-marketed the stuff --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: -- and carried on with it, but we didn't do that -- I'm not involved with that, but -- The department stores and things over there were still pretty intact -- pretty much in -- in -- operational.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And I remember buying a beautiful evening purse, which I still have, hand-sewn with silk, bamboo trims and everything, for my wife. Also sent home a Japanese saddle, general saddle. Also sent home a Japanese rifle. And interesting about a Japanese rifle --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Small?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Well, not only that, but the emperor had a flower, if I don't remember the --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Lotus blossom.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Lotus blossom. And every one of them had been ground off.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: If you had one with that lotus blossom on them, then you had a prize. And mine had no lotus blossom. But those are the things in Japan. And then of course when we got ready to -- I got enough points in December to be discharged back to the States. So as a final program in Japan for the group that I was with, in this little town that we were visiting -- and they had sugar piles and all this other stuff, good stuff, that we're -- we had to confiscate to make sure it wasn't black-marketed. There was a -- there was a little place, and there was a theater. And we thought, "What can we do to remember this?"

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: So we talked with the mayor and everything about putting on a New Year's ceremonial Japanese-style costume and all that could be supplied show. So we went to this captain of the thing. We told the captain we'd like to go to New Year's Eve, take a 6x6, and go to this town with our own food and stay there that night and go to this -- and see this show. It happened. We arrived at that town New Year's Eve. They had that place painted beautifully, colors. It almost -- still wet almost, but it was still -- and they put on a ceremonial with all their old-style instruments --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: -- and their costumes, for about an hour and a half.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Is that right?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: I remember that. A New Year's party I'll never forget. And just us GIs sat there, and we ate our own bread. None of their fish or anything like that.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And that was a -- that was a final thing. Of course, they shipped out of Japan on the 1st of January, 1946. A couple other stories in Japan. Do you ever -- do you know this -- I don't know. The lady here might not like this, but the latrines in Japan are made to accommodate 10, 15, 20 people.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And everything is separated.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Communal, yeah.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Well, it's all then delivered by -- by cart and oxen, driven to the local farmer, and then it's put on the two buckets on a crossbar on their shoulder, and it's hand-dippered on each one of the vegetables.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Is that right?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: You cannot stand the odor. The carrots would grow a diameter about like a grapefruit and be that big, but we couldn't eat them -- we were just not allowed to eat any of that stuff. But that's the way their stuff is.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Is that right?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: But they were very clean, very clean people. But that's -- that's other stories. So to finish up my story -- well, anyway, we shipped out of Japan, and you could only bring certain amount of money back. And I happened to have a watch that I sold, and I bought the watch in New York before I left New York City. And I sold it to a Japanese fellow that wanted it so bad, and he -- I don't know. I think I probably got about 85 or a hundred dollars for it.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And the --

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Let's see that cup there, Mr. Brown. Show us that. This is your cup, and you've engraved all the spots that you visited on it, all --

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Ships.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: -- the ships, the countries --

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: The main cities, the countries. My Army serial number and my name on the bottom. It's a fantastic cup.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: It is.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Carried many -- the coffee in here, surprised the cup still lived. Black coffee.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Pretty tough coffee, huh?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah. Pretty bad coffee.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Yeah. I know that.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: We left Japan in January of 1946, and I got on a ship called -- the FREMONT AP

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And we shipped out of Japan. I don't remember the town. And we got halfway through the Pacific Ocean on the way home, and the ship engine quit. And we sat adrift for about 24 hours while they fixed the engine. Thank God, the war was over with.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Yeah, really.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: We wound up in Seattle, Washington. Took a train across the United States. Wound up in Chicago. Disbarked -- let's see. Took a train from Chicago to Detroit. Arrived home January 27, 1946. Went overseas a little over 18 months. My daughter was -- I only seen her when she was about three weeks old.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Two years old already?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah. Two years old. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: That's tough.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And lo and behold -- this is a military secret. My second daughter was born nine months and one day after I got home.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Even made a laugh out of her. Carol.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: That story is a lot of basically what happened to me, and I'm not elaborating on any of the sour stuff or the war stuff other than the fact that we don't need wars. And one of the outstanding things, I think, in the war other than the devastation and the -- and the killing and the maiming of the people was the children, starving children. And we were not allowed to feed them in our outfit.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Why is that?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Well, it was part of the rules. I remember in the Philippines, in some parts of -- other parts of the world, that the children would be on the outside of our camp while we were eating our meals or wherever we were, and the rule was you're not to feed them, but we did. I never smoked in my life. My cigarettes went for chocolate bars. My chocolate bars went to the kids.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Is that right?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: And I didn't get any money for them. And I wound up in Paris a number of times without money, and I had to borrow 10 dollars or so, but Paris was one of the things. But that -- other than people that we left behind us, left over there, around the world, why, that's a sad part.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: The rest of it, I -- I look back on it as a great adventure, but I certainly wouldn't want anyone else to do it and have to do it. And I feel sorry for these people that have to do these things nowadays.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, you mean in the service?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: The service.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: In the service.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: They don't know that.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: No matter what part of the service you're in, it's no ball of fire. No game. It's real life. But that's life. You live. So I've been self-employed all my life, and that's the way it is. Running auto kinetic and -- in a way, it was -- I was born and raised on a farm in a way. You learn a lot. We were born -- where I lived, there was no electricity or things like that. Dirt roads. And you walked two and a half miles to school. Nobody believed me until the time I took my daughters back there and finally told them where the school was and measured out. Two and a half miles. Snow, even with the telephone wires in the winter. And the telephone wires sing to you. Yeah. A lot of stories. Back where I was -- I visited there a few years ago, and it hasn't changed in 60 years or 70 years.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Where was this at now?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: In Lysander. In Syracuse, New York area.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Oh, Syracuse. That's where you're originally from?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah. Out in the country. Same store on the corner that -- when I went to school.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Is that right?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: In June -- June, I'll be 82, so that's a long time ago.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: That's a long time ago.

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Same cemeteries there, too.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: (laughter) Way back in the 1600s.

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Is that right? Way back that far?

sp.speaker: William Brown
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. Way back. Fantastic stories. Well, I think I'm (inaudible).

sp.speaker: Dan Packer
sp.p: Okay. Thank you, Mister -- (Conclusion of interview.)
